, /PRNewswire/ -- Interloc Solutions, a provider of innovative consulting services and mobile solutions, today announced the launch of Informer EdgeSync for MAS\. This new breakthrough synchronization solution enables organizations to upgrade to MAS with Zero Downtime\. Built on the proven Interloc Informer Server platform, EdgeSync eliminates the traditional barriers to MAS migration by keeping Maximo 7\.6 running while organizations upgrade and fully validate their MAS environment\.

EdgeSync synchronizes data between existing Maximo 7\.6 environments and MAS at the Maximo Business Object \(MBO\) level, ensuring updates flow seamlessly between systems without expensive database mirroring tools or manual ETL processing\. Users can continue operating in 7\.6 while MAS is tested and validated—relieving pressure on cutover timing and enabling migration only when the new system is fully ready\. The database-agnostic, profile-driven solution provides resilient store-and-forward pipelines for enterprise grade reliability\. In addition to zero-downtime upgrades, EdgeSync provides real-time hot-standby system capability as part of a disaster recovery strategy\.

\"Our goal is simple: keep our customers online, efficient, and moving forward\. Informer EdgeSync for MAS, along with our growing technology suite, is designed to remove complexity, eliminate downtime, and give organizations the real-time control they need to operate at their best,\" says Mike Watson, CEO at Interloc solutions\.

This news builds on Interloc's Informer portfolio and extends the capabilities of Informer\. Informer EdgeSync for MAS is available for on-premises, cloud, and hybrid deployments\. EdgeSync is included at no additional cost when migrating to MAS within the Interloc Cloud\.

**About Interloc**

Interloc Solutions is an IBM Platinum Business Partner and brings over 20 years of experience helping asset-intensive organizations modernize and optimize their enterprise asset management environments\. We specialize in IBM Maximo and Maximo Application Suite \(MAS\), supporting upgrades, implementations, and long-term platform strategy\. Interloc's secure Cloud Services deliver scalable, reliable hosting for mission-critical systems\.

, /PRNewswire/ -- King County's Facilities Management Division \(FMD\) officially went into production with version 9\.0 of the IBM Maximo Application Suite \(MAS\) earlier this summer\. This upgrade marks a major milestone in the County's commitment to modernizing asset management processes and leveraging advanced technology to better serve its customers\.

Interloc Solutions partnered closely with FMD throughout the planning, configuration, testing, and implementation phases to ensure the GO LIVE transition was seamless and disruption to daily operations was minimal\. The collaborative effort included extensive data validation, staff training, and a carefully coordinated cutover strategy to safeguard service continuity\. In addition to upgrading to \"MAS\" Interloc's cloud services division migrated King County to Microsoft Azures cloud\.

\"This update is a significant improvement to our asset management process,\" said John Shepard, FMD Asset Manager\. \"FMD is taking advantage of cutting-edge technology that not many have access to yet\. Being able to pioneer this update is a nod not only to our team's willingness to improve the way we do things, but also to how our partners view the importance of the work we do\.\"

With MAS 9\.01, FMD gains a more complete and real-time view of its asset portfolio\. The new system delivers advanced tools for asset tracking, lifecycle management, and performance monitoring—capabilities that were not previously available\. It also establishes a single, authoritative source of asset-related data, enabling more accurate reporting, streamlined auditing, and improved decision-making\.

The successful launch positions FMD as a technology leader among public-sector facilities management organizations, setting the stage for continued innovation in asset management and service delivery\.

**MAS 9\.01** is now live and ready for users to experience\. To learn more, visit interlocsolutions\.com or contact Scott Peluso for inquiries\.

About King County FMD  
King County is the nation's 12th largest county, with nearly 2\.3 million residents\. The county spans 2,300 square miles, from the shore of Puget Sound to the crest of the Cascade Range\. The Facilities Management Division \(FMD\), part of King County's Department of Executive Services, oversees and maintains more than 50 real estate assets spanning the entirety of King County\. The division employs about 400 people across nine sections, including 12 cross-functional teams\. Learn more at kingcounty\.gov\.

About Interloc  
Since 2005, Interloc Solutions, an IBM Gold Business Partner and the largest independent IBM Maximo Enterprise Asset Management systems integrator in North America, has been helping clients and partners realize the greatest potential from their enterprise asset management investment\. Interloc provides application hosting, innovative consulting, and managed services for the global Maximo community\. Interloc has enhanced the implementation and adoption of Maximo through its transformative Mobile Informer solution, which is currently in use across a wide range of disciplines and industries— including U\.S\. Federal Agencies, Utilities, Transportation, Airport Operations, Manufacturing, Healthcare, and Oil and Gas\. With experience in all versions of Maximo and a consulting organization of highly qualified technology and maintenance professionals, Interloc excels in delivering comprehensive, best-practice Maximo EAM consulting services and mobile solutions\.

Published 11:50 am Thursday, September 25, 2025

Both the Snoqualmie and North Bend city councils have approved a new agreement that includes the dismissal of Snoqualmie’s lawsuit against North Bend\.

The renewal interlocal agreement — approved by Snoqualmie on Sept\. 15 and North Bend on Sept\. 16 — states that the Snoqualmie Police Department will provide services to the city of North Bend through March 31, 2026\. The King County Sheriff’s Office will provide policing services to North Bend starting April 1, 2026\.

The interlocal agreement also resolves litigation between the two cities\. In June, Snoqualmie sued North Bend seeking damages after the two cities had a disagreement about what was owed based on past interlocal agreements\.

North Bend has been contracting with Snoqualmie for police services since 2012, with the last interlocal agreement before this year being put forth in 2019\. That agreement expired at the end of 2024, and was renewed in January to last until May 31\. In those five months, North Bend City Council discussed what they would like to do for future police services\. On May 6, council members voted unanimously in favor of contracting with the King County Sheriff’s Office instead of Snoqualmie\.

North Bend formally terminated Snoqualmie on May 20, but said police services were supposed to continue for 18 months, as stated by the original interlocal agreement’s 18-month termination notice\. This would have ended Snoqualmie’s police services to North Bend in November 2026\.

Snoqualmie disagreed and, on May 27, Snoqualmie Mayor Katherine Ross notified North Bend Mayor Mary Miller that without a new contract, Snoqualmie would cease to provide police services to North Bend starting June 1\.

Snoqualmie and North Bend did enter into a revised interlocal agreement at that time\. But then, on June 26, Snoqualmie filed a complaint for declaratory relief and damages, a type of civil lawsuit, in King County Superior Court\.

The two cities have now come to an agreement that will allow them to avoid a lawsuit and the additional costs that would result from it\. By the end of July, Snoqualmie had already spent $24,418 on legal costs, according to the agenda bill\.

Per the September interlocal agreement, North Bend will pay Snoqualmie a monthly fee of ​​$236,306, retroactive to June 2025, through the end of the year\. That monthly fee will increase to $294,000 per month for January, February and March 2026\.

This is more than North Bend was paying Snoqualmie under the May interlocal agreement, which had a monthly fee of $219,849\.

During North Bend’s meeting, councilmembers noted that they were frustrated by the last several months, but excited to be moving forward\.

“I am excited and ecstatic about that, primarily because I think it will allow the legislative bodies of our two cities to stop feeling like we are fighting with each other and begin to rebuild trust and relationships,” said Councilmember Mark Joselyn\. “Because of our proximity and relationship to each other, it’s a very important relationship, and it has suffered as a result of this\.”

## Cities of Sparks, Reno Approve Interlocal Agreement for Shared Fire Chief Services

Municipal leadership in northern Nevada is shifting toward regional resource sharing as the cities of Sparks and Reno officially approve an interlocal agreement for shared Fire Chief services, according to local reporting from KTVN\. Under the terms of the newly approved arrangement, the City of Sparks will reimburse the City for the shared administrative framework, creating a collaborative leadership structure across adjacent municipal fire departments\.

## Understanding the Interlocal Agreement Mechanics

The operational framework establishes a cooperative model where executive oversight is pooled between the two neighboring jurisdictions\. Rather than maintaining entirely separate administrative commands for top-tier fire leadership, the municipalities are leaning into structural efficiency\. Sparks will reimburse the City of Reno under specific financial guidelines outlined in the pact, ensuring that neither municipality absorbs an unbalanced fiscal burden while sharing high-level municipal expertise\.

So what does this mean for daily emergency response? According to municipal policy documents, the arrangement targets executive-level administrative alignment rather than frontline crew consolidations\. Stations will maintain their local staffing and deployment protocols, but the administrative command structure overhead will operate under a unified vision\. It is a pragmatic pivot for two growing Nevada cities sharing porous borders and overlapping infrastructure corridors\.

## Regional Cooperation and Economic Realities

Shared municipal services have gained traction across the American West as cities grapple with rising operational costs, equipment inflation, and pension liabilities\. By splitting the cost of a top-tier fire executive, both Reno and Sparks can direct more tax dollars toward frontline apparatus, gear replacement, and station maintenance\.

Critics of shared executive models often point to potential conflicts of interest or divided loyalties during major multi-jurisdictional emergencies\. When two fast-growing cities compete for resources during simultaneous major incidents, administrative strain can test the limits of a single chief\. However, proponents argue that formal interlocal agreements actually codify cooperation, replacing informal handshakes with legally binding protocols that streamline mutual aid long before an emergency strikes\.

## Broader Civic Context in Northern Nevada

This administrative alignment arrives alongside other regional civic initiatives aimed at community engagement and public safety infrastructure across the region\. While municipal leaders finalize the operational details of the shared fire command, civic programs continue to engage local residents, including recent initiatives inviting Nevada students to create road safety artwork for a Carson City mural\.

New safety plan released by NDOT with the aim of keeping drivers safe on Nevada roads

As the agreement takes effect, administrative teams from both Sparks and Reno will monitor executive workload metrics and cost-sharing accuracy to evaluate the partnership’s long-term viability\. The success of this joint venture could well serve as a blueprint for other municipal departments seeking collaborative solutions in a tight fiscal climate\.

# Tacoma City Council eyes joining Pierce County’s Unified Regional Approach on homelessness

TACOMA, Wash\. — City leaders in Tacoma could soon join a countywide effort to coordinate homelessness services as Pierce County seeks to replace a patchwork of local responses with a regional system\.

The Tacoma City Council is expected to consider a resolution Aug\. 25 expressing its intent to help launch Pierce County’s Unified Regional Approach, or URA, which is built around shared data and cooperation among governments and service providers\.

**SEE ALSO \| Tacoma council weighs removal of boulders that deter homeless camps amid mixed reactions**

Pierce County Councilmember Jani Hitchen presented the proposal to the council during a study session earlier this week\.

“Tacoma coming on board as the largest population in the county, along with the majority of services happening, is huge for us,” Hitchen said\. “Tacoma is ready to take that next step, and I'm thrilled\.\"

The resolution would commit Tacoma to working with other Pierce County governments on the regional system\. If approved, city staff would begin developing an interlocal agreement that would define the specifics of its role\.

“We all are going to use the same database\. We are all going to use coordinated entry to homelessness, where people who are unhoused all know where to go,” said Tacoma Council Member Sarah Rumbaugh, the main sponsor of the resolution\.

The effort comes as Tacoma continues to shoulder much of the county’s homelessness response\. Pierce County’s 2025 Point-in-Time Count identified nearly 3,000 people experiencing homelessness\. Tacoma hosts about 85% of the county’s shelter beds, and 76% of people counted were staying in a Tacoma shelter\.

County officials said homelessness crosses municipal boundaries and requires a response that does the same\. Under the proposal, local governments, nonprofit organizations and service providers would share information and coordinate services rather than operating largely independently\.

“The goal is to make sure that for anyone who enters homelessness in Pierce County, that there is a response and that it's the same kind of response,” Hitchen said\.

Pierce County began developing the regional approach in 2022\. Pierce County, Fife, Gig Harbor and Lakewood have since adopted resolutions expressing their intent to participate in launching the system\.

A central part of the proposal is expanded use of the Homeless Management Information System\. Using the same database could improve the accuracy of countywide information and help providers identify available shelter space and gaps in services\.

**RELATED \| Traction builds for regional approach to homelessness in Pierce County**

Unlike the King County Regional Homelessness Authority, Pierce County’s system would not be established as an independent agency or pool participating governments’ money into a single fund\. Instead, Pierce County would oversee the initiative while governments coordinate through interlocal agreements\.

“Everybody will be able to see what we're spending money on,” Hitchen said\. “They'll know what we're doing from the very beginning, and they'll know how much different cities and towns are contributing\.\"

The details of each participating city's responsibilities have not yet been settled\. Those provisions are expected to be established through the interlocal agreement developed by the participating governments\.

Pierce County spends about $50 million every year on homelessness programs\. In Tacoma, the Neighborhood and Community Services Department has budgeted $25\.5 million this biennium, but that does not include associated costs for first responders, such as medical calls to encampments by firefighters\.

# Board of Commissioners Recap: Aug\. 4, 2026

At its Aug\. 4 regular meeting, the Buncombe County Board of Commissioners approved several actions aimed at expanding park access, strengthening partnerships with local governments, and supporting economic development\. Commissioners accepted new grant funding for river access improvements, updated an interlocal agreement with the Town of Woodfin to advance greenway construction, and authorized participation in a state Building Reuse Grant to support Southeastern Container’s planned expansion\.

**Helene Recovery: NC Parks & Recreation Trust Fund**  
The Board of Commissioners approved $284,368 in grant funding for the Buncombe County River Access Enhancement Project\. The project will replace vulnerable, informal river access with three ADA-accessible, flood-resilient boat launches at Bent Creek River Park, Glen Bridge River Park, and Hominy Creek River Park\. The County has already budgeted $163,638 in the FY27 Glen Bridge River Park Boat Launch Replacement project and obligated $120,730 in FEMA Public Assistance funds for recovery work at Hominy Creek River Park\.

This award comes from the NC Parks and Recreation Trust Fund’s Helene Recovery Fund, which supports public recreation projects that assist communities recovering from Hurricane Helene\. No additional County funding is required\. Parks & Recreation will partner with NC Fish & Wildlife and FEMA to design and construct the new launches\.

**Interlocal Agreement Addendum: Buncombe County & Town of Woodfin**  
The Board of Commissioners approved an addendum to the existing interlocal agreement with the Town of Woodfin\. The original 2017 agreement named the County as Woodfin’s agent to conduct and manage greenway construction along the French Broad River, with Woodfin supporting the project through reimbursement resolutions and borrowing for two sections\.

Since then, both parties have identified two feasible greenway projects in Woodfin\. The addendum clarifies roles and responsibilities, identifies the specific greenways, commits the County to constructing them, and confirms the County will turn over ownership to the Town of Woodfin to permanently maintain them\.

Read the entire addendum\.

**Economic Development Update: Building Reuse Grant for Southeastern Container**

Southeastern Container, an advanced manufacturer located in the Enka Commerce Park, announced in February that it will expand its facility with a $31 million investment and 12 new full-time jobs with an average wage of $32\.90 per hour\.  
To support this expansion, NC Commerce awarded the company a $100,000 Building Reuse grant\. The grant requires a 5% local match of $5,000, which will be budgeted next year\. The Board of Commissioners approved a resolution authorizing the County Manager to coordinate with Southeastern Container and participate in the Building Reuse program\.

Read the resolution\.

**Good News: Best in Category National Recognition**

During the July National Association of Counties \(NACo\) conference, which included more than 3,000 counties nationwide, Buncombe County earned seven 2026 Achievement Awards\. The County also received its first-ever Best in Category award for Economic Service’s Staff Development Training program—one of only 18 such honors given this year\.

Read more about the NACo awards\.

**FY2026 Property Tax Settlement and Order of Collection for Current Fiscal Year**

Pursuant to NCGS 105-373, the Board of Commissioners approved the annual settlement of property tax collected in the previous fiscal year\. Following approval of the Tax Collector's Annual Settlement for the preceding year, the Board adopted the Order of Collection for the current fiscal year property taxes pursuant to NCGS 105-321\. Buncombe County’s regular property collection rate was 99\.66% as of June 30, 2026\.

# Pottawattamie County board backs updated interlocal agreement

\(Council Bluffs\) -- Pottawattamie County officials have backed an updated agreement to ensure the county continues to have first responder communication ahead of its transition to a statewide system\.

By a 4-0 vote at its regular meeting Tuesday morning, the Pottawattamie County Board of Supervisors approved renewing an Interlocal Agreement for Cooperative Use of the Wireless Area Network with Orion and heard a brief update on the county's transition to the Iowa Statewide Interoperable Communications System \(ISICS\)\. In December 2025, the board approved an agreement with Motorola Solutions for equipment and technology upgrades needed to join the statewide system before authorizing up to $6 million in general obligation bonds to help finance the project\. While indicating the ISICS transition is still on schedule, County Communications Captain Sam Arkfeld says the current Orion agreement wasn't going to line up with the projected completion\.

\"The timing of this particular agreement is coming up prior to the completion of the \(ISICS\) project,\" said Arkfeld\. \"So, I would not say that the project is behind, it's just that the two did not align with each other\.\"

Thus, Arkfeld says the new agreement would be on a month-to-month basis until the county can officially transfer to ISICS\. Supervisor Susan Miller says the month-to-month agreement will be a good way to transition the county from its current situation to ISICS\. She ultimately made the motion to approve the new agreement\.

\"I think this is a good safety net to put in place and be transparent with Orion that they've been a great partner to work with and that we're leaving on good terms,\" said Miller\. \"But, we need to work together as we unwind our relationship with Orion and switch over to ISICS\.\"

Overall, like most projects, Arkfeld says there have been a few \"bumps in the road\" as the county works to transition to the statewide system\. He notes they are still currently working to finalize tower surveys\.

\"One on a particular building did not pass the structural analysis, so we're looking at some alternatives,\" said Arkfeld\. \"Currently, we're probably going to look at replacing the tower and then seeing if the building itself can structurally support a new tower and the load that would have\.\"

Arkfeld says they are also working to get a survey done for the tower in Crescent\. He added they were holding a project meeting Tuesday afternoon, after which he would be able to provide the board with more information\. More from Tuesday's Pottawattamie County Board of Supervisors meeting is available with this story at kmaland\.com\.

# Carahsoft to Distribute Panoptica's Threat Intel Platform

- **Carahsoft and Panoptica have teamed up to distribute the latter’s Watchtower platform to the public sector**
- **Panoptica’s platform offers SOCMINT and chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities**
- **The ****2026 Intel Summit**** will explore agentic AI, OSINT and more**

Carahsoft Technology and Panoptica Technologies have partnered to make the latter’s Watchtower artificial intelligence-enabled threat intelligence platform and other capabilities available to government customers\.

*As intelligence agencies look to sharpen their analytical edge, the Potomac Officers Club’s **2026 Intel Summit** on Sept\. 24 will bring together industry and government leaders to unpack the tools driving that shift\. Panel discussions will dig into analytics, agentic AI, open source intelligence and more\. **Save your seat now** to be part of the conversation\.*

## How Will Carahsoft Support Panoptica Through the Partnership?

Carahsoft said Tuesday it will serve as Panoptica’s public sector distributor and deliver the company’s Watchtower platform through its reseller ecosystem and contract vehicles, including NASA Solutions for Enterprise-Wide Procurement V, The Interlocal Purchasing System and OMNIA Partners contracts\.

## What Does Panoptica’s Watchtower Platform Offer?

Panoptica’s Watchtower platform uses AI-powered agents to accelerate threat detection and intelligence workflows for tactical-level intelligence delivery\. The models are trained on data from security professionals operating in high-risk environments and incorporate social, cultural and political context to support analytical accuracy\.

The platform includes chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities that help analysts identify the cause of terrorist or hostile activities and assess the probability of downstream events\. It also includes social media intelligence capabilities that identify coded language, slang, symbols and emojis used by terrorist organizations to track emerging threats\.

## What Did Carahsoft & Panoptica Officials Say About the Partnership?

“Panoptica’s platform empowers analysts with tools designed to accelerate threat detection, enhance intelligence analysis and improve operational effectiveness,” said Michael Adams, senior sales director and program executive for AI solutions at Carahsoft\. “Together with our reseller partners, Panoptica and Carahsoft are helping Government organizations strengthen mission outcomes and enhance situational awareness through Panoptica’s innovative solutions\.”

Panoptica co-founder and CEO Martin So said the partnership will help get mission-critical software into the hands of the warfighter quickly amid an increasingly complex threat environment\. He noted that Carahsoft’s relationship with the intelligence community and expedited procurement system will help the company deliver solutions in a timely manner\.

## What Are Carahsoft’s Other Public Sector Tech Partnerships?

Carahsoft has continued to expand its public sector partner ecosystem through a series of additional agreements\. The company has teamed up with Rocketgraph to bring a high-performance graph analytics platform to federal, state and local government agencies\.

Carahsoft has also partnered with Rhino\.ai to distribute an automated system discovery and generative AI-based modernization platform to public sector agencies, while US AI has selected Carahsoft to deliver its Intelligent Computing Platform to government customers\.

Rounding out its recent lineup, Carahsoft will serve as the public sector distributor of Zenity, expanding government access to its AI agent governance platform\.

# Pensacola Bay Center entertainment campus plans hit snag over city-county agreement

PENSACOLA, Fla\. -- The future of the Pensacola Bay Center was the center of attention on Thursday at the county's committee of the whole meeting\.

For more than an hour, commissioners discussed and asked questions about how to move forward with the project\. No major decisions were made\.

But a recently discovered memorandum of understanding from 1982 is revealing the City of Pensacola may legally have more of a say in what goes into the Bay Center than the county thought\.

County attorneys have now drafted a new memorandum of understanding that's getting even more attention\. It's because commissioners didn't know it was drafted in the first place\.

The interlocal agreement would give the city the final say on anything that happens on that land\.

Some of the commissioners said they were unaware such an agreement was even drafted\.

Commissioners discussed the 3-phase approach to turning the area around the Bay Center into an entertainment campus\.

\"It was all about the Bay Center, so what are the next steps?\" District 4 Commissioner Ashlee Hofberger said\. \"What property are we prioritizing, what property are we looking at renovating, and what next steps are going to be taken with moving forward with renovating that entire facility and property?\"

Progress stalled when some of the commissioners brought up concerns about an interlocal agreement between the city and the county\.

It was approved by county legal back in June, but none of the commissioners saw it\.

\"The proposed draft being approved by county legal is one thing, but that's not the board,\" District 5 Commissioner Steven Barry said\. \"I don't know if my colleagues approve; I certainly didn't give a stamp of approval to that\.\"

\"I didn't even know about the interlocal agreement until today; I didn't even know about the meetings,\" District 3 Commissioner Lumon May said\.

WEAR News got a copy of the draft agreement\.

It was published on the Pensacola City Council agenda for their next meeting\.

The city confirmed the mayor pulled the agreement from the council agenda\.

The agreement referred to an MOU from 1982 that shows the city of Pensacola owns most of the land where the improvements would be made\.

The agreement would require the county to get final approval from the city of Pensacola and FDOT for any of the improvements to the Bay Center or additional construction that goes on the land\.

\"The interlocal agreement yesterday, which got a lot of brouhaha,\" District 2 Commissioner Mike Kohler said\. \"I'm not really worried at this point; I think we can probably get to something reasonable, but I was caught off guard by that too\. I think that should have had more discussion before today because it's out on social media and the city is going to decide, and we're going to pay and all this nonsense\. It doesn't help the project as a whole\.\"

Commissioner Barry said the board seemed interested in moving forward with designing the improvements to the Bay Center but said the project cannot move forward until the city and the county work out the interlocal agreement\.
